answer: African textiles differ in their construction, histories and social uses. Kente is traditionally made from woven strips associated with Asante and Ewe communities; Ankara refers to printed cotton shaped by global trade and African design choices. In eastern Africa, kitenge and kanga are distinct terms, with kanga often carrying written messages.

sources.title: Africa fashion: cloth of a continent

facts.fact: The V&A describes Ankara as printed cotton linked to industrial European attempts to reproduce Indonesian batik.
The V&A identifies kente as strips of handwoven cloth traditionally associated with Asante and Ewe communities.
The Met describes an Asante kente wrapper built from narrow woven strips sewn together.
The Met catalogues an Ewe kente prestige cloth dated circa 1930–1950 from Ghana and western Togo traditions.
The Met describes Asante prestige cloth panels composed of as many as 24 woven bands in one example.
The British Museum describes kanga as rectangular printed cloth with inscriptions, often sold and worn in matching pairs.
The Met explicitly labels one Ghanaian kente object’s cultural attribution as ‘Asante or Ewe (?)’, reflecting uncertainty.
